I know you asked for charts but someone else already hooked you up:

Unless something has drastically changed in the last five years, integrated graphics cards are easily ten to fifty times slower than your basic affordable video card. Nobody at all would ever recommend you "stay with integrated' unless you have a very niche use like super-low power requirements, or you never play games.

There's a lot of factors, but the two biggest are memory contention, and the fact that they're designed to be as cheap as possible. The cheap part is fairly straight-forward, so let's hit memory contention:

All your system memory is on a bus (a set of wires shared by multiple computer chips/systems). A bus connects many things, but only TWO can talk to each other (one sender to one receiver) at any moment.

Any time your computer is on, that bus has to be shared across all your programs, all your operating system's internal processes (network, time scheduling, etc), and any hardware that access memory. (*AGP was a "hack" technology that directly connected to your CPU without a bus, but as a consequence could also freeze your CPU if the hardware/driver messed up.)

When you have something extremely high bandwidth, and time sensitive (variations cause noticable jitter), you do not want to be contending with other things for access. Videocards are exactly that case. So it's been forever ago since they've moved to having their own memory (called "VRAM" or video ram). Even when video ram was slower than system ram, it was faster for a videocard to use that onboard ram because it didn't have to contend to use it. It had exclusive 100% access. Moreover, the further away physically a part is, and the more "steps" (buses and chips) it has to go through, the more the latency is going to be. Like a plane having multiple layovers at airports vs a direct flight.

Now with an onboard videocard, the single most important thing--memory bandwidth--is gone! System memory CANNOT be accessed from multiple locations at the same time. So any time something else fires off (your soundcard buffering, a packet coming in, your operating system interrupting everything to do some time keeping like scheduling the next set of processes to run), that videocard bandwidth is going to die.

I should also mention that the reasons memory bandwidth is the most important thing are that 1) CPUs are 100 to 1000 times faster than memory now and growing steadily. 2) Everything about drawing a 2-D or 3-D scene involves tons of memory reads and to a lesser extend writes. Every texture, painted thousands (if not tens of thousands!) of times, is read, pixels-by-pixel from memory every frame. And frames have to be done in milliseconds. Lots of memory reads, plus tiny amount of time to do it in, means HUGE memory rate to satisfy the GPU's hunger!

p.s. This isn't the most well-crafted post I've ever made, but I hope it provides a little insight and that I've hit a few keywords that you can then Google/Wiki for some more insight into how this electronic beasts work.
